evidence.claim: McNary’s name crossed state lines with a lumber company, part of a relocation that brought hundreds of employees into this Arizona community.

evidence.claim: McNary’s name crossed state lines with a lumber company, part of a relocation that brought hundreds of employees into this Arizona community. In 1924, Cady Lumber moved its entire operation from McNary, Louisiana, to the Arizona community then called Cooley. For marketing purposes, the company obtained federal permission to bring the name along. An earlier name, Cluff Cienega, recalled Benjamin Cluff’s hay harvests for Fort Apache in 1879 and 1880. The mill closed after a fire in 1979. The community is on the Fort Apache Indian Reservation, where the White Mountain Apache Tribe operates local bus service.

evidence.claim: The name Eagar was a postal compromise, reached after the first postmistress tried to give the community a name expressing her hope for local unity.
evidence.quote: The first postmistress, Emma Goldsbrough Udall, wanted to name the town "Union", in a desire for eventually combining the town with other towns such as Amity and Springerville, to unite the small community.

evidence.claim: The name Eagar was a postal compromise, reached after the first postmistress tried to give the community a name expressing her hope for local unity. Emma Goldsbrough Udall proposed Union, hoping eventually to combine the community with places including Amity and Springerville. The postmaster general rejected Union as too common. She then submitted Eagarville to honor the Eagar brothers, only to have it shortened to Eagar. The town’s plan also reflects its Mormon settlement: square blocks and broad streets followed the general City of Zion concept, with irrigation supplied from the Little Colorado River through the Big Ditch.
evidence.quote: the blocks and streets were slightly smaller, approximately 500 foot square and 90 foot wide, respectively.

evidence.claim: The Little Colorado River runs through Greer, a White Mountains community reached by Highway 373. Originally called Lee Valley, the settlement took the shorter name Greer when its post office was built. A separate transport history lies west of town, in remnants of the Apache Railway. Logging operations began in 1918; the White Mountain Scenic Railroad began operating on the line in 1964 and ceased in 1976. The Maverick-to-McNary track was removed in 1982.

evidence.claim: Big Lake holds rainwater and snowmelt at 9,000 feet in the White Mountains. The reservoir was created by damming a small tributary of the Black River and belongs to the Salt River watershed. Its setting combines subalpine grasslands and forest at the base of Mount Baldy. Winter changes the road journey here: snow closes access roads, generally from December to early April. The lake’s cold water supports rainbow, cutthroat and brook trout.

flags: ADOT describes a 67-mile loop plus the Greer spur, while material maps 82.2 miles including the McNary approach. Do not equate the mapped total with the designated loop.
Material orders Eagar before Greer despite Greer lying west of Eagar. Retained that order with an explicit return west from Eagar before the Greer spur and lake circuit; this adds backtracking.
SR 273 cache disagrees internally on whether its southern terminus is the SR 261 junction or Big Lake; prose describes access without asserting an exact terminus.
Dropped current claim that Greer is Arizona’s highest town: the cache uses inconsistent town/community rankings, including a conflicting McNary ranking. No elevation superlative retained.
Closure guidance comes from the cached Big Lake article, not a current operator bulletin. Checked date records review of supplied cache only; exact 2026 closure dates are not verified.
National Forest Scenic Byway designation in material is not independently established by this cache; state scenic designation is supported.
All current moments and their coordinates retained; Big Lake added with its cache coordinates.
